title: Playlist Engine
tagline: You write a program that keeps a list of songs. Your program can add a new song, take one out, put the songs in order, and print the whole list.
objectives: Make a list, and get one thing out of it by its position.
Add to a list, take something out of it, and put it in order.
Read a few lines of Python that use a list, and say what they will print.

config.headline: One name can hold a whole set of things.
lines: Last lesson every box (a variable) held one thing: one name, one price, one number of seats. Today one name holds a whole row of boxes, in an order you decide. Python calls that a LIST.

A shopping list is a list. So is a seating plan. So is the set of songs a show plays, in the order it plays them. Once a set of things has one name, you can count them, add to them, take one out, and put them in order — and you never have to type them out again.
Nothing in this lesson makes a sound. A playlist here is a set of song titles you type, and your program moves those titles around.
You already have everything you need to start. A list is made the same way a box is made: a name, an = sign, and what goes in it. The only new part is what goes on the right of the = sign.
Here is the hour, in order.
1. You watch a short film with no sound. It shows a list as a rack of numbered boxes.

2. You play the Prediction Match. Somebody else in this room, at another computer, sees the same few lines of Python as you, at the same moment. You each choose what you think the code will print. You both lock your answer in, and then the code really runs. You are not told who you are playing until the Match ends. Instead you each get a call sign, a made-up name like Director 3. Your call sign is the only name they see, and their call sign is the only name you see.
3. You watch a second short film. After it come three builds. In the first the program is written for you; by the third you are filling in the gaps yourself.
4. You get twelve minutes to build your own Playlist Engine, with five songs you choose yourself.
5. You can try three extra jobs, if there is time.
6. You finish with two short things: one question to answer, and three lines of Python to put in the right order. Then a screen asks you how the hour went.

config.title: Say what the code will do, before it does it
config.intro:
Working out what code will print, before you run it, is hard. The only way to get good at it is to say your answer before you find out.

There are six rounds. Somebody else in this room sees the same few lines as you, at the same moment. You each choose what you think it will print, you both lock it in, and then the code really runs on this screen.

**Getting one right is worth no points and getting one wrong costs you nothing.** You get the badge for the Match whatever you predict, as long as you play all six rounds. Being right is between you and your opponent.
steps: You are given a **call sign** — a made-up name like Director 3. Your call sign is the only name they see, and their call sign is the only name you see.
Both screens show the same code. You each pick what you think it prints and lock it in.
The code really runs, and both predictions sit beside the real answer.
Rounds 5 and 6 are on things nobody has taught you yet. The screen tells you before each of those two rounds starts, so you will know when you are guessing.
config.finishLabel: Leave the Match and carry on with the lesson

rounds.lead: This prints a whole list in one go. Look closely at what Python puts around it.
options: Opening Night Curtain Up Last Bus Home

Opening Night
Curtain Up
Last Bus Home
rounds.teach: Printing the whole list prints it the way Python writes a list down: square brackets round the outside, commas between, and speech marks round every title. A list is one thing with one name, and that is how Python shows all of it at once.

rounds.lead: This one reads one title out of the list and prints it. Count carefully, then type exactly what you think appears.
rounds.teach: Counting starts at 0, so playlist[0] is Opening Night and playlist[1] is Curtain Up. The number in the square brackets is a POSITION, never a count — this is the single thing people get wrong most often, all year.

rounds.lead: Read both lines before you choose. The second one asks Python a question about the list.
rounds.teach: len( ) counts how many things are in the list, so it says 3. The last position is 2, because counting starts at 0. The number of things and the last position are always one apart.

rounds.lead: This one adds a title before it counts. Watch what happens to the number.
rounds.teach: .append( ) adds a new thing on the END and leaves everything already there alone, so the list grows from 2 to 3. That is the difference between adding and replacing: playlist = ["Last Bus Home"] would have thrown the other two away and left one.

rounds.ask: Have a guess. What will this print?
rounds.lead: Nobody has shown you this yet. Look at it, decide what you think happens, and lock it in.
options:
Opening Night
Curtain Up
Last Bus Home
rounds.teach: This is a LOOP. It takes the list one thing at a time, puts each one into a box (a variable) called song, and runs the line underneath once for each of them. That line is pushed in by four spaces, and those four spaces are what put it inside the loop. Three titles in the list means three trips round the loop, and three printed lines. You build one of these yourself later in the hour.

rounds.ask: Have a guess. What will this print?
rounds.lead: Nobody has shown you this either, and this one catches nearly everybody.
rounds.teach: This one has a trap in it. .sort( ) really did put the list in order — the list itself is now ['Curtain Up', 'Opening Night']. But .sort( ) hands nothing back, so the box called answer gets None, Python's word for nothing. The box called answer never holds the playlist. To see a sorted list, put playlist.sort() on a line of its own, then print(playlist). The second film shows this again, now that you have watched it happen.

sideShow.name: Margo
sideShow.alt: Margo, a cartoon theatre critic in a fur stole, peering over half-moon glasses
sideShow.open: Ah. An empty stage. I am Margo, and I review whatever is put in front of me. At the moment that is nothing.
lines: The silence continues. A bold artistic choice. Two stars.
I have now been staring at this waiting screen for longer than most plays last.
Nothing is happening, and it is happening beautifully. One star.
In forty years of criticism I have never seen a stage this committed to being empty.
I would leave, but there is nowhere for me to go. I live here. This screen is my whole life.
Half a star. And the half is generous.
echo: "{you}". I shall be honest: I have no idea what to do with that.
sideShow.exitLine: THEY'RE HERE! Five stars! A triumph! I take back everything! Go, go — do not keep them waiting!
sideShow.leaveLine: Leaving early? Off you go. I shall still be here.

errorWords.name: Python does not know a box (a variable) with that name. Check the spelling on this line matches the name you gave the list further up.
errorWords.type: Python has been asked to put two different kinds of thing together, and it will not. If you joined a number onto words with a +, put str( ) around the number first — that is what lets the + join it on. If you sorted a list with both numbers and words in it, Python cannot say which of them comes first.
errorWords.badinput: Python could not read that line at all. Check the speech marks come in pairs, the brackets come in pairs, and the line starts where the lines around it start.

errorWords.index: That line asks for a position in the list that is not there. Counting starts at 0, so the last position is one less than the number of things in the list.
errorWords.attr: Python does not know that word after the dot. Check the spelling of the word straight after the dot — append, remove and sort are the ones you have.

errorWords.value: Python could not use the thing in the brackets. If this was a remove line, the title has to match one that is really in the list, capital letters and all.

config.title: Twelve minutes to build your own Playlist Engine, with five songs you choose.
config.intro:
Every program so far has used somebody else’s songs. This one is yours: five real songs you choose, and a program that does five different things to them.

One of the jobs uses Python nobody has shown you yet, so here it is. import random, on the very first line, switches on Python's picking tools. random.choice(playlist) then picks one title from the list at random — it can be a different one every run.

There are no ready-made lines to drag across on this card: you type the program yourself. At the top of the card are the five jobs your engine has to do. Every time you press RUN, each job says done as soon as your program really does that job.

builds.goalLine: Write a playlist engine that does five things to five songs of your own.
builds.brief: Start with five real song titles you would put in a show. The five jobs your engine has to do are numbered above, and each one says done as soon as your program really does that job.

features.label: It ADDS a song, so the list ends up longer than the one you typed.
features.nudge: Your list is not growing. Look for the line with append on it, and check the title you are adding is inside speech marks.

features.label: It TAKES ONE OUT, so one of your songs is gone by the end.
features.nudge: Nothing is being taken out. remove needs a title spelled exactly as it appears in your list — including the capital letters.

features.label: It picks a song AT RANDOM and prints a line about it.
features.nudge: Nothing in your program picks a song at random yet. Check that random.choice is on the line that prints Tonight, and that the very first line of your program says import random.

features.label: The list ends up in A to Z order.
features.nudge: Your list is not in order at the end. Look at where your sort line is: anything that changes the list AFTER it can put it out of order again.

features.head: now playing

consoleLabels.title: The console
consoleLabels.idle: Nothing has run yet. Press RUN when you are ready.
consoleLabels.nothingLead: Your program ran, and it printed nothing at all.
consoleLabels.errorLead: Python stopped, and this is exactly what it said:
consoleLabels.offline: Python did not load just now. Tell whoever is in the room, and press RUN again in a moment.

errorWords.name: Python does not know a box (a variable) with that name. Check the spelling on this line matches the name you gave the list further up.
errorWords.type: Python has been asked to put two different kinds of thing together, and it will not. If you joined a number onto words with a +, put str( ) around the number first. If you sorted a list with both numbers and words in it, Python cannot say which of them comes first.
errorWords.badinput: Python could not read that line at all. Check the speech marks come in pairs, the brackets come in pairs, and the line starts where the lines around it start.
errorWords.eof: Something was opened on that line and never closed. Look for a bracket or a speech mark with no partner.
errorWords.unindent: The lines inside the loop are not all lined up with each other. Every line inside a loop starts four spaces in, and they all start at the same place.
errorWords.index: You asked for a position in the list that is not there. Counting starts at 0, so the last position is one less than the number of things in the list.
errorWords.attr: Python does not know that word after the dot. Check the spelling of the word straight after the dot — append, remove and sort are the ones you have.
errorWords.timelimit: That program was still going after a few seconds, so it was stopped. Something in it is repeating and never finishing.
errorWords.other: Python stopped at the line named above. Read that line again, slowly, and check every bracket and every speech mark.
errorWords.value: Python could not use the thing in the brackets. If this was a remove line, the title has to match one that is really in the list, capital letters and all.
errorWords.syntax: Python could not read one of your lines. Look at the line named above. Check that every bracket you opened is also closed, that every speech mark has a partner, and that any line under a colon starts four spaces in.

config.help: There are three optional jobs. None of them is worth points and nothing here is saved. Pick one from the list, or press the button at the bottom that says “Leave the extra jobs and carry on with the lesson”. If you leave a job half done it starts again from the beginning next time.

builds.title: Job 1 — print only the titles marked Live
builds.whiff: A taste of next year: the program decides which ones to print.
builds.goalLine: Print only the titles that have the word Live in them.
builds.brief: A loop can look at each title and decide whether to print it. The word if is how a program chooses. You meet it properly next year — this is one small taste of it.

lines.t: playlist = ["Opening Night", "Curtain Up (Live)", "Last Bus Home", "The Long Way Round (Live)"]

builds.matchedSay: Two of the four titles printed. The if line is what made the loop choose.

builds.title: Job 2 — the list in reverse
builds.whiff: One line puts the whole list back to front.
builds.goalLine: Print the list with the titles in the opposite order.
builds.brief: Lists have a job called reverse, and it works exactly like sort: it changes the list itself and gives you nothing back.
builds.matchedSay: The list is reversed. The extra line, the one you did not use, would have printed None — for exactly the same reason sort does.

builds.title: Job 3 — what else can go in a list?
builds.whiff: This one is an experiment: a list will hold anything you put in it.
builds.goalLine: Put a number and some words in the same list, and print each one on its own line.
builds.brief: A list will hold anything, and it will hold different kinds of thing at the same time. Build it and see what comes out.
builds.matchedSay: Three lines printed, and one of them is a number. A list will hold anything — but ask for a position that is not there and the program stops.
